A novel theoretical method for predicting the effects of lighting colour
temperature on physiological responses and indoor thermal perception
Amir Omidvara,*, Arianna Brambillab
aDepartment of Mechanical Engineering, Shiraz University of Technology, Shiraz, Iran
bSchool of Architecture, Design and Planning, The University of Sydney, NSW, Australia
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: The neural integration of information from different sensory modalities, known as multisensory integration, is a
Lighting colour phenomenon that can affect people’s thermal perception. Previous experimental research validated the hue-heat
Hue-heat effect hypothesis as one of the contexts of multisensory integration. The present research introduces the equivalent
Physiological response
metabolic rate as a novel parameter to include the hue-heat effects in conventional thermal comfort models. To
Thermal comfort
this aim, an analytical expression was developed for calculating the equivalent metabolic rate according to the
Metabolic rate
correlated colour temperature (CCT) of the ambient light and implemented in both steady and transient thermal
comfort models. The modified models were validated against published experimental data. The effects of lighting
colour on physiological responses and thermal perception were then investigated for four different CCTs under
three different indoor temperatures. The simulated results showed that any deviation from CCT 5000 ​K evokes
thermophysiological responses and alters the people’s thermal sensation compared to what is expected by
standard thermal comfort models. The maximum and minimum lighting effects were observed at 4000 ​K and
6500 ​K CCT, respectively. The results also showed that thermal perception is more sensitive to CCT changes in
warm environments. Furthermore, it is predicted that the thermal sensation could be changed up to 0.8 units by
changing the lighting colour, while the skin temperature and wettedness could change up to 0.8◦C and 0.14,
respectively. This paper demonstrates that the novel equivalent metabolic rate parameter can be successfully
used to predict the thermal sensation under varying lighting environments, making a substantial contribution to
multisensory integration.

In this section, the proposed improved transient two-node model is
used to predict and study the combined effects of indoor temperature
and lighting CCT on the body’s thermo-physiological regulatory re-
sponses. The physiological factors considered in the present study are
skin temperature, core temperature, skin wettedness, and blood perfu-

three different indoor temperatures (21◦C, 24◦C, and 27◦C) and four
different CCTs (2800 ​K, 4000 ​K, 5000 ​K, and 6500 ​K). In each indoor
temperature condition, the body’s physiological responses to stepwise
changes in lighting CCT are simulated numerically by the improved
Gagge’s model.
